current_example.problem:
Consider the arc of the curve $x=y^2$ that lies between $y=0$ and $y=2,$ as shown below. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14133198/assets/30c2b0000055802166e5bdf8ec3e305d83e65ac960043f66463702952d91e4d6.png)
current_example.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} x \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})=2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2})\sqrt{1+{(2y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
